flashcards.q: What is the central design decision when authoring an MCP server for your own codebase?
flashcards.a: Tool granularity: too fine (ORM-shaped, one tool per CRUD op) burns the agent's step budget assembling primitives; too coarse (one god-tool with an action string) forces the model to guess an internal vocabulary. Right size is one tool per workflow a caller actually wants done.

flashcards.q: Give the tool-selection accuracy numbers that justify keeping tool count low.
flashcards.a: Benchmark data shows ~19/20 correct at 20 tools falling to complete failure past ~107 tools. A pooled unfiltered catalogue scored 13.62% in one stress test. GitHub Copilot cut 40 tools to 13 and gained a 400ms latency drop plus 2-5 point accuracy improvement.

flashcards.q: How do you decide tool vs resource vs prompt for something in your own codebase?
flashcards.a: Who decides to use it. Tool: the model decides at runtime (variable scope, side effects). Resource: the host attaches it deterministically (fixed reference material). Prompt: a human explicitly triggers it (repeated fixed-shape request).

flashcards.q: What is the tell that a tool is too fine-grained (ORM-shaped)?
flashcards.a: Naming it requires "and" (get and filter and sort) -- the agent is doing a join or assembly step your code could do in one deterministic call.

flashcards.q: What is the tell that a tool is too coarse-grained (a god-tool)?
flashcards.a: Naming it requires "or" (create or update or delete or list) -- a decision got hidden inside a string argument instead of the tool boundary, and the model must guess the internal action vocabulary from one opaque schema.

flashcards.q: How should an MCP tool's error message be written differently than a human-facing exception?
flashcards.a: Name the exact rule violated, show a valid example, and name the tool/call that unblocks the caller. A model has no source file to open like a human debugger would -- the error string is the only signal it gets.

flashcards.q: Where should a tool's error content go in the MCP response, and why?
flashcards.a: Inside the tools/call result as isError:true content, never as a raised JSON-RPC protocol error. Protocol errors kill the client mid-await; isError content is an observation the model can read and route around.

flashcards.q: Why should a secret never be a tool argument?
flashcards.a: Any value passed as a tool argument is held in the model's own context and can be echoed into a later tool call, a log line, or the final response. Secrets should be read server-side from environment or a credential store at call time.

flashcards.q: Why does a mutating tool need both dry_run and an idempotency key -- aren't they redundant?
flashcards.a: No. dry_run previews the effect before it happens (builds trust, catches wrong plans). An idempotency key makes a retried call return the stored result instead of double-executing. One doesn't substitute for the other.

flashcards.q: How do you derive an idempotency key for an MCP tool call, and what's the trap?
flashcards.a: hash(session_id, tool_name, sorted(args)). The trap: forgetting to sort args means logically identical calls with differently-ordered keys hash differently, silently defeating the mechanism.

flashcards.q: Name the observable symptom of the over-tooling failure mode.
flashcards.a: Tool-selection collapse: the model calls a plausible-sounding tool name that doesn't exist in tools/list, or picks the wrong one of two similarly-named tools. It can even make an unrelated, previously-fine server misfire once total schema token load crosses a threshold.

flashcards.q: List the three fixes for the over-tooling failure, cheapest first.
flashcards.a: 1) Namespace by service prefix (asana_search vs jira_search). 2) Curate to real workflows instead of auto-wrapping every endpoint. 3) Progressive disclosure (list_capabilities/invoke) or topic-scoped sub-servers past a few dozen genuine operations.

flashcards.q: What token reduction does Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP / progressive disclosure pattern achieve?
flashcards.a: Roughly 150,000 input tokens down to about 2,000 for the same task, a 98.7% reduction, by having the model write code that calls tools instead of loading every schema up front.

flashcards.q: What are the two separate evals needed to test an MCP server, and why can't one substitute for the other?
flashcards.a: Selection accuracy (does the model call the right tool with valid arguments -- exposes granularity problems) and task success (did the outcome actually complete correctly -- exposes schema/error-message problems). A server can pass one and fail the other.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build an MCP server for an internal tool?
flashcards.a: When exactly one agent in one process will ever call it. A bare function call reaches the same code in microseconds with no schema validation and no subprocess/network round trip; MCP earns its cost only when a genuinely different consumer needs the same capability.
